title: Week 1: Build a talking box

series.title: Physical AI Lab: Cardboard Robot (4 week course)
series.summary: A four-week build, one session a week. Week 1: a cardboard box that talks, with a mouth that moves. Week 2: a turning neck. Week 3 (optional, bring your own Raspberry Pi): it runs on its own, no laptop or cables. Week 4: demo day. Most of every session is spent in Deepgram's voice studio, not on the glue gun.

summary: A cardboard robot whose mouth moves when it talks. The box comes ready-built, so attendees spend 15 minutes finishing it and about 40 minutes in Deepgram's voice studio: writing its personality, choosing its voice, tuning Flux turn-taking and giving it skills.
detail: Your robot box arrives already folded with its servo glued in. You draw its face, hook up the paperclip that opens its mouth, and wire it to a small breadboard. Then the rest of the session happens on this page: give it a personality, try different Deepgram voices, tune how Flux decides you've finished talking, and let it check the weather and read a calendar. The mouth opens and shuts in time with its voice. Finish by filming a clip of your robot talking.
outcome: A cardboard robot on your table that holds a real conversation in a voice and personality you chose, moves its mouth as it speaks, and checks the weather, plus a clip of it to share.
artifact: A talking cardboard robot running the attendee's own Deepgram voice agent, and a short video of it.
prereqs: A laptop with Google Chrome. Safari and Firefox can't talk to USB devices.
A free Deepgram account and API key. Use the sign-up QR code at your table.
A USB port on your laptop. USB-C only laptop? We have USB-C to micro-USB cables.
Everything else is on the table.

slides.title: Talking Robot Box
bullets: A cardboard robot that talks, and its mouth moves when it does.
15 minutes building. About 40 minutes making it talk with Deepgram. 5 minutes showing off.
No coding.
slides.note: Hold up a finished robot and have it say hello. That's the whole pitch. Keep the build moving: the voice studio is the main event.

slides.title: What each robot needs
bullets: ☐ 1 × robot box, already built: folded, mouth flap hinged, tab glued in, servo glued down
☐ 1 × Raspberry Pi Pico (Pico H, Pico 2 or Pico 2 W, with pins), loaded with the robot program
☐ 1 × half-size breadboard with + and − power rails
☐ 2 × male-to-female jumper wires (signal and ground)
☐ 2 × male-to-male jumper wires (servo power)
☐ 1 × USB-to-2-pin power lead, and a spot on the table's USB charger
☐ 1 × micro-USB data cable (not charge-only), USB-C or USB-A to match your laptop
☐ 1 × jumbo paperclip
☐ Tape and a marker
Bring: a laptop with Chrome, and your Deepgram key
slides.note: Before class, helpers build every box (about 5 minutes each, so batch them the day before): fold the 8×8×8 inch box, tape the bottom shut, cut off the two front side flaps, glue the top front flap shut, glue a cut-off flap piece inside the bottom flap as a tab, and hot-glue an MG90S servo to the floor near the front with its horn on and facing up. Load and test every Pico with Connect robot. Each table gets a multi-port USB wall charger and a power strip. Helper table: spare built boxes, spare data cables (the one people forget), USB-C adapters, 2–3 spare Picos, extra paperclips, one glue gun for fixes.

slides.title: Finish your robot
bullets: Put a strip of tape across the top flap and draw its eyes.
Bend the paperclip into an L.
Hook one end through a hole in the servo horn, and push the other end through the tab inside the mouth.
Turn the horn gently by hand: the mouth should open and shut.
slides.note: Done when: turning the horn by hand opens and closes the mouth. If it binds, bend the paperclip, don't force the servo.

slides.title: Wire it up
bullets: Orange servo wire to GP15 (pin 20, bottom left with the USB at the top), with a male-to-female jumper.
Red to the breadboard's + row, brown to the − row, with male-to-male jumpers.
One jumper from the − row to the Pico's GND (pin 23).
Power lead into the + and − rows, then into the table's USB charger.
Nothing goes on VBUS (pin 40). Then plug the Pico into your laptop.
slides.note: Hold the Pico with the USB port at the top and the Raspberry Pi logo facing you. Pin 1 is top left. Why the breadboard: a laptop's USB can't power the servo reliably, and when it moves fast the Pico resets and the page loses it. The charger powers the servo; the Pico only sends the signal. Helpers check every board before anyone plugs in: red on +, brown on −, ground jumper to pin 23, nothing on pin 40. Aim to have every robot plugged in by minute 18.

slides.title: Meet the Deepgram Voice Agent
bullets: Flux listens, and works out when you've finished talking.
A language model thinks, using the personality you write.
Flux speaks, in the voice you choose.
One live connection does all three, in real time.
Your page turns the loudness of its voice into mouth movement.
slides.note: Two minutes, no more. Point at the How the pieces fit diagram further down the page.

slides.title: First words
bullets: Paste your Deepgram key.
Quit Thonny if it's open, then press Connect robot.
Set the mouth, slowly and in order: shut first, then open. Stop before it buzzes.
Press Wiggle the mouth to check.
Press Start talking and say hello.
slides.note: The sliders move the servo live. Fast drags or pushing past the end of the mouth make it buzz and strain. Sensitivity sets how much the mouth opens for quiet words; it never goes past the open setting.

slides.title: Give it a personality
bullets: Press Stop, then rewrite Personality: who is it, how does it talk, what does it care about?
Keep its replies to one or two sentences. Short sounds natural out loud.
Change the first thing it says.
Start again. Does it stay in character when you try to throw it off?
slides.note: Ideas to offer: a grumpy pirate box, a nervous first-day intern, an over-excited tour guide for The Hub, a box that's sure it's a fridge.

slides.title: Find its voice
bullets: Try three different voices, one at a time.
Same personality, different voice: which one fits?
Listen for pace, warmth, and how it says your name.
slides.note: All of these are Deepgram Flux voices, generated live as it talks.

slides.title: Turn-taking with Flux
bullets: Set Patience to 0.5. Pause halfway through a sentence. Does it jump in?
Set it to 0.9 and try again. Notice the wait before it answers.
Flux listens for when you're done talking, not just for silence.
Pick the setting that feels most like a real conversation.
slides.note: This is the part people remember: turn-taking is what makes a voice agent feel human or robotic.

slides.title: Give it skills
bullets: Ask: what's the weather in Tokyo?
Ask: what's on my calendar today?
Watch the Tool lines in the transcript. That's a function call.
The agent decides when to call a function. Your page runs it and hands back the answer.
slides.note: The weather is real (Open-Meteo); the calendar is a made-up sample, so nobody's real schedule is read out.

slides.title: Show it off
bullets: Ask it the weather somewhere far away.
Try to make it laugh.
Film a 20-second clip and share it with #RobotLunchLab.
slides.note: Set up one well-lit corner with a plain background for filming.

slides.title: Week 2: give it a neck
bullets: Bring your robot back next week.
We add a second box, a servo and a turntable bearing, so the head turns.
And your own power bank, so later it can run without a wall socket.
slides.note: Robots can stay on the shelf at The Hub between sessions.

flow.title: Make it talk with Deepgram (40 min)
Your robot's voice studio
flow.note: Plug the robot in, then work through the voice studio slides above, one at a time.

troubleshooting: Connect robot shows "No compatible devices found": the Pico isn't running MicroPython and the robot program yet, it's in BOOTSEL mode (a drive called RPI-RP2 or RP2350 is open), or the cable only charges. Swap the cable first.
Connect robot does nothing at all: you're not in Chrome. Open the page in Chrome on the laptop.
It says the board did not answer: the Pico isn't running the robot program. Unplug it, plug it back in and connect again. If that fails, a helper swaps the Pico.
Another program is using the port: quit Thonny and close other tabs with this page, unplug the Pico, plug it back in, and connect again.

The page says the robot reset while talking or when you move a slider: the servo is pulling power from the Pico. Check red goes to the + row, the charger is plugged in, nothing is on pin 40, and the ground jumper is in. The page reconnects on its own once it's back.
The servo buzzes or twitches fast at one end: shut or open is pushing past where the mouth can go. Move it back 2 or 3 steps with the − and + buttons.
The mouth moves the wrong way: swap the shut and open numbers.
The servo twitches on its own: the ground jumper from the − row to pin 23 is missing.
The robot talks to itself: keep "Speaker is inside the box" switched on.
It cuts you off: raise Patience. It's slow to answer: lower it.
No sound: turn up the laptop volume and check the output device in system settings.
Deepgram stopped the session: check the key was pasted whole, and that the account has credit.
